title: Four Windows on One King
subtitle: Four voices, one king, and the art of seeing between the lines
era: How historians reconstruct Harsha, c. 606-649 CE and after
region: Kannauj, Thanesar, Banskhera, Aihole and Chang'an
moral: Truth grows stronger when sources are compared, not worshipped.

sources.citation: Aihole Prashasti of Ravikirti, trans. Franz Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica VI (1900-01)
sources.note: Rival Chalukya inscription that records Harsha's Narmada setback.

sources.citation: Banskhera Copper Plate of Harsha, Epigraphia Indica IV; Harshacharita and Da Tang Xiyu Ji compared
sources.note: Primary source set for triangulating court, legal and travel records.

sources.citation: Hans T. Bakker, The World of the Skandapurana (Brill, 2014), ch. 6; Max Deeg, 'How Buddhist Are Buddhist Pilgrimage Accounts?' (2016)
sources.note: Recent source-critical studies of Bana and Xuanzang.

panels.shot: dramatic split-screen wide, four vertical 'windows' framing different visions of the same crowned king in mid-distance

dialogue.text: Bāṇa, Xuanzang, copper plates, an enemy’s boast and Chinese annals—all swear they knew Harsha. Stand between them, and the king fractures into four. How do historians choose which Harsha to believe?

panels.shot: slow push-in on a wooden table strewn with manuscripts and rubbings under lamplight

dialogue.text: This is not the story of one king’s life, but of how we know it. To reach Harsha across thirteen centuries, historians sit with four very different witnesses.

panels.shot: close-up of the palm-leaf manuscript with ornate script and miniature illustration of court

dialogue.text: The first is a court poet: Bāṇa, author of the Harshacharita. He writes in scented ink, under royal protection, and claims he will tell the truth while every sentence flatters his patron.

panels.shot: medium shot, over-the-shoulder, imagining Bana at court as the manuscript fades into a lived scene

dialogue.text: Bāṇa’s Harsha is a wonder child, a just avenger, a scholar-king who restores order to north India. His prose dazzles with similes, battles and processions, yet the king never loses or falters.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on a specific line, the tiny chaturanga reference, finger pointing to it

dialogue.text: Between the flourishes, small details hide. Bāṇa casually mentions chaturanga, a war game of footmen, horses, elephants and chariots. A single line, yet proof that such games already trained minds in strategy.

panels.shot: medium shot, the copper plate in foreground, poet’s manuscript fading behind it

dialogue.text: Set Bāṇa aside, and a second witness speaks in metal. Harsha’s copper plates—like the Banskhera charter—record land grants, legal phrases, and the titles the king accepted when no poet was watching.

panels.shot: close-up on the copper plate inscription, selective focus on 'Parama-maheśvara' title

dialogue.text: Here Harsha is not the Buddhist patron of legend, but Parama-maheśvara, ‘supreme devotee of Maheshvara’, a Shaiva king. The same ruler, yet a different face, cut in copper for Brahmin donees.

panels.shot: wide shot, superimposed double image of Harsha as Shaiva king and Buddhist patron behind the scholar

dialogue.text: Did Harsha change religions? The record does not say so directly. Instead, historians see a king who could sponsor Buddhist assemblies, revere Śiva, and deploy each identity to bind different allies.

panels.shot: medium shot, the Chinese scroll being unrolled, background hinting at Chang’an

dialogue.text: A third window opens far from Kannauj. Xuanzang, the monk-pilgrim whose Da Tang Xiyu Ji later guided Chinese editors, writes as an eyewitness to Harsha’s court, yet through the eyes of a Buddhist seeker.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye imagined view of Harsha’s great religious assembly, with Xuanzang in the crowd

dialogue.speaker: harsha_s_sources
dialogue.text: Here, the king appears almost as a bodhisattva, yet the copper plates still call him Maheshvara’s devotee.

panels.shot: close-up on marginal note citing modern scholarship beside Xuanzang’s text

dialogue.text: Modern scholars warn: pilgrimage stories are not neutral mirrors. Xuanzang praises monasteries and miracles, notes taxes and punishments, yet passes quickly over conflicts that do not serve his religious aim.

panels.shot: medium shot, the Aihole inscription rubbing being pinned beside the other sources

dialogue.text: Then comes a rival’s voice. At Aihole, the poet Ravikirti celebrates Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas, and briefly, almost casually, tells how Harsha was checked on the Narmada’s northern bank.

panels.shot: wide shot blending an imagined clash at the Narmada with Harsha’s Sources watching

dialogue.text: Bāṇa never reaches this moment. His narrative breaks earlier, leaving Harsha unbeaten. Ravikirti’s single verse, meant to glorify Pulakeshin, instead reveals that even a great north Indian king met limits.

panels.shot: medium shot, Harsha’s Sources adding a final Chinese historical chronicle to the table

dialogue.text: After Harsha’s death, Chinese dynastic histories record what Indian inscriptions leave faint: embassies, shifting rulers, and a crisis in north India, where no single king holds Kannauj for long.

panels.shot: close-up on Harsha’s Sources’ thoughtful face lit by the glow of all four windows

dialogue.text: None of these voices simply lies, and none tells the whole story. Each reveals and conceals according to its purpose: praise, donation, devotion, rivalry, or imperial record.

panels.shot: wide shot, all four windows now aligned, their images of Harsha overlapping into a composite silhouette

dialogue.text: By comparing Bāṇa’s tale with copper charters, setting Xuanzang beside Ravikirti, and reading them against Chinese histories, historians reconstruct a Harsha who is more complex than any one portrait.

panels.shot: slow pull-back to a vast archive hall, tiny figure amid shelves of sources old and new

dialogue.text: In this hall of echoes, the lesson outlasts the king: truth in history grows not by worshipping a single testimony, but by holding many partial windows together and asking, again and again, what they hide and what they show.
